analysis.one_liner: Lets employers pay some workers above their union-negotiated contract wage.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee in May 2019 and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors joining after introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so that a union contract could not stop an employer from paying an individual employee more than the contract's wage scale allows [S2, S3]. Many union contracts set one pay structure for everyone in the bargaining unit; this bill would let companies go around it for favored workers [S2, S3]. It was introduced by Senator Marco Rubio with two other Senate Republicans and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it received no further action for the rest of the Congress [S1, S3, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers at unionized companies gain the ability to pay individual workers above the contract scale without renegotiating the contract — flexibility they can use to reward preferred employees or to undercut the union's role as the one negotiator of pay. Some individual employees could receive higher pay than their contract provides.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unionized employers and some individual workers

how_it_helps.text: Amends the National Labor Relations Act to provide that neither a union's exclusive representation nor the terms of a collective bargaining agreement entered into after enactment can prohibit an employer from paying an employee greater wages or compensation than the contract provides [S2, S3].
The bill's stated purpose is 'to permit employers to pay higher wages to their employees,' framed as letting successful employees be rewarded beyond a union-negotiated scale [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions lose a tool of collective bargaining: contracts that set a single wage structure for a unit become partly unenforceable, weakening the union's leverage at the next negotiation. Workers who benefit from negotiated step scales and uniform raises could face divided pay structures, with raises negotiated for the group eroded by individual side deals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Labor unions and their negotiated pay structures

drawbacks.text: Union contracts commonly cap individual pay as part of a bargain that secures a wage floor and raises for everyone in the unit; allowing employers to bypass the cap for selected workers can undermine the collective bargaining that set that floor in the first place [S2, S3].

The bill applies to any compensation an employer wants to give above contract, with no requirement that the higher pay be tied to performance, so the discretion lies entirely with management rather than with employees [S3].
The bill received no committee hearing or markup in the 19 months between referral and the end of the Congress, so its practical effects on union contracts were never examined on the record [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promises higher pay for individual workers, and some employees at union shops could genuinely earn more than their scale. But the mechanism removes a provision unions negotiate deliberately — a shared pay structure — and hands the discretion to management, which is why union-aligned groups treated the bill as a way to weaken organized labor rather than a straightforward raise. Because it never advanced past referral, none of these effects was ever tested in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Marco Rubio introduced the bill on May 23, 2019, joined by Senators John Cornyn and John Barrasso [S3, S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1, S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the negotiated wage structures at unionized workplaces are unaffected, since the bill never advanced. Employers who wanted the freedom to pay around a union contract gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat or additional member cosponsored the bill at any point in the Congress [S3, S4].

industries.note: The bill would override a core term unions negotiate — a single wage structure for the bargaining unit — reducing their leverage with employers. Union members' negotiated raises and step scales depend on that structure, so the union's interest here runs alongside its members'.

Employers would gain the right to pay above contract at their own discretion, without renegotiating. That flexibility can reward individual workers, but it also lets management divide the workforce and bypass the union as the negotiator of pay — a gain that comes at the cost of the collective bargaining workers rely on.
